name: Expansion of Physical Capacity
consequences: Increasing suites from 8 to 12 would accelerate participant enrollment and event capture but risks overextension if pilot metrics like false alarm rates and annotation throughput are not met. Deferred expansion preserves fiscal discipline but may limit data diversity and longitudinal analysis scope.
options: Expand to 12 suites immediately to maximize data capture potential
Delay expansion until pilot data confirms operational efficiency
Implement modular renovations to allow phased capacity increases
review: Expanding physical capacity risks overextension if pilot metrics like false alarm rates and annotation throughput are not met, potentially straining resources without proven efficiency gains.

name: Staffing Ratio Optimization
consequences: Adjusting technician-to-suite ratios could improve response times during events but may increase labor costs. Overstaffing risks budget overruns, while understaffing jeopardizes participant safety and data integrity during critical monitoring windows.
options: Hire additional full-time technicians to reduce shift overlap and fatigue
Implement a hybrid model of full-time and on-call staff to balance coverage and cost
Introduce automated alert triage systems to prioritize technician interventions
review: Automated alert triage systems may reduce manual workload but could introduce latency in critical event responses, undermining the facility's safety-critical operations.

name: Sensor Integration Strategy
consequences: Adding new sensor modalities enhances physiological resolution but increases data complexity and storage demands. Over-reliance on untested technologies risks compatibility issues with existing workflows.
options: Integrate high-density EMG arrays to improve event localization accuracy
Pilot contactless biometric sensors to reduce participant discomfort
Prioritize sensor fusion algorithms to streamline multi-modal data correlation
review: Sensor fusion algorithms may improve data coherence but require extensive validation against gold-standard PSG metrics to avoid introducing systematic biases.

name: Recruitment Criteria Adjustment
consequences: Broadening inclusion criteria could increase participant numbers but may dilute the homogeneity of parasomnia phenotypes. Narrowing criteria improves data specificity but risks enrollment shortfalls.
options: Include participants with subthreshold parasomnia symptoms to boost enrollment
Implement tiered eligibility based on event frequency and clinical severity
Target high-risk occupational groups (e.g., shift workers) for specialized recruitment
review: Targeting high-risk occupational groups may accelerate enrollment but could introduce confounding variables related to sleep deprivation and circadian disruption.

name: Financial Flexibility Mechanisms
consequences: Securing alternative funding sources diversifies risk but may introduce external oversight constraints. Relying on a single grant increases vulnerability to funding cuts.
options: Pursue industry partnerships for sensor development while retaining publication rights
Establish a reserve fund from early-stage data licensing agreements
Implement dynamic budget reallocations based on quarterly performance metrics
review: Dynamic budget reallocations risk destabilizing long-term operations if short-term priorities conflict with methodological validation goals.

name: Data Accessibility Framework
consequences: Expanding data sharing accelerates scientific impact but heightens privacy risks. Restricted access preserves ethical compliance but limits collaborative innovation.
options: Create a controlled-access portal for approved researchers with anonymized physiological data
Develop synthetic data models for algorithm training while retaining raw data internally
Partner with institutional repositories for curated dataset releases
review: Synthetic data models may fail to capture rare event patterns, reducing their utility for validating semi-automated triage tools.

name: Participant Engagement Strategy
consequences: Enhancing incentives with tiered compensation based on retention directly increases enrollment stability but risks inflating costs without guaranteed participation rates. A community-building initiative with shared sleep hygiene workshops could improve compliance but requires dedicated staff time and may dilute focus on clinical objectives.
options: Enhance incentives with tiered compensation based on retention
Implement bi-weekly feedback sessions to improve participant satisfaction
Create a community-building initiative with shared sleep hygiene workshops
review: Tiered compensation risks cost overruns without measurable engagement gains, while feedback sessions may divert staff from core data collection tasks.

name: Regulatory Compliance Framework
consequences: Adopting a proactive ethics review process with pre-approval for all data-sharing agreements streamlines future collaborations but delays initial protocol implementation. Quarterly external audits by independent boards strengthen credibility but add administrative overhead that could strain early-stage operations.
options: Adopt a proactive ethics review process with pre-approval for all data-sharing agreements
Establish a real-time compliance dashboard for audit readiness
Conduct quarterly external audits by independent ethics boards
review: Proactive ethics reviews may delay project timelines but reduce later regulatory hurdles, while external audits increase transparency at the cost of operational agility.

name: Data Annotation Process
consequences: Introducing a dual-rater system with randomized cross-validation improves inter-rater reliability but doubles annotation labor costs. Machine-assisted annotation with human oversight for critical events accelerates processing but requires algorithm development and validation that may not align with current AASM criteria.
options: Introduce a dual-rater system with randomized cross-validation
Implement machine-assisted annotation with human oversight for critical events
Schedule bi-weekly annotation workshops to standardize criteria
review: Dual-rater systems improve reliability but increase labor costs, while machine-assisted annotation introduces technical complexity without guaranteed accuracy.

name: Sensor Calibration Protocol
consequences: Scheduling daily calibration checks with automated alerts for deviations ensures data integrity but consumes technician time. Deploying redundant sensor arrays to cross-validate data streams reduces single-point failure risks but increases equipment procurement and maintenance costs.
options: Schedule daily calibration checks with automated alerts for deviations
Use reference participants for periodic recalibration
Deploy redundant sensor arrays to cross-validate data streams
review: Redundant sensors add upfront costs but reduce data loss from single-point failures, while reference participants complicate logistics without clear reliability gains.

name: Staff Training Program
consequences: Conducting immersive simulation training for emergency scenarios improves response preparedness but requires significant time and resource investment. Rotating staff between data annotation and clinical monitoring roles enhances cross-functional expertise but may reduce specialization in critical tasks.
options: Conduct immersive simulation training for emergency scenarios
Offer specialized certification in parasomnia diagnostics for all technicians
Rotate staff between data annotation and clinical monitoring roles
review: Simulation training enhances preparedness but diverts from operational tasks, while role rotation risks diluting technical proficiency in core functions.

name: Participant Retention Tactics
consequences: Providing flexible scheduling for extended stays with adjusted compensation directly addresses retention but complicates logistics. Offering post-study health assessments as a retention incentive builds goodwill but requires additional clinical resources and may introduce bias in participant selection.
options: Provide flexible scheduling for extended stays with adjusted compensation
Establish a peer support network among participants
Offer post-study health assessments as a retention incentive
review: Flexible scheduling may complicate operational planning, while post-study assessments risk prioritizing participant satisfaction over scientific objectivity.

name: Emergency Response Protocol
consequences: Designating a 24/7 on-site medical responder with trauma training ensures immediate care for critical incidents but increases staffing costs. Conducting monthly emergency drills with local services improves coordination but requires external resource allocation and potential disruptions to research operations.
options: Designate a 24/7 on-site medical responder with trauma training
Implement a rapid-escalation protocol for high-risk events
Conduct monthly emergency drills with local fire and rescue services
review: 24/7 medical presence increases staffing costs but ensures immediate response, while drills enhance preparedness at the expense of operational continuity.

name: Facility Safety Configuration
consequences: Adjusting safety features could enhance participant security but might require additional resources. A downstream effect could be increased maintenance costs or potential delays in facility setup.
options: Install additional motion-sensor alarms in high-risk zones
Conduct biannual safety drills with participants and staff
Upgrade to fire-resistant materials in all common areas
review: Increasing safety measures may raise initial costs but minimizes incident risks.

name: Participant Engagement Protocol
consequences: Enhancing engagement strategies could improve data quality but might divert resources from core research activities. A downstream implication is potential burnout among staff managing extended participant interactions.
options: Implement structured daily debriefing sessions with participants
Introduce gamified compliance incentives for event reporting
Establish peer support networks among enrolled participants
review: Gamified incentives risk diluting scientific rigor if not tightly aligned with data collection goals.

name: Data Storage Optimization
consequences: Improving storage efficiency could reduce long-term costs but might require upfront investment in infrastructure. A downstream effect is potential complexity in data retrieval workflows.
options: Adopt tiered storage architecture with cold storage for archival data
Implement real-time data compression during acquisition
Establish cross-institutional data mirroring agreements
review: Tiered storage may complicate data access protocols without clear scalability benefits.

name: Ethical Compliance Integration
consequences: Strengthening ethical oversight could enhance public trust but might slow down research timelines. A downstream implication is increased administrative burden on the PI and coordinator.
options: Integrate continuous ethics training for all staff members
Create a participant advisory board for feedback loops
Implement automated consent renewal reminders
review: Participant advisory boards may introduce conflicting priorities without clear governance structures.

name: Staff Training Enhancement
consequences: Expanding training programs could improve technical proficiency but might reduce immediate operational capacity. A downstream effect is potential knowledge silos if training is not standardized.
options: Develop cross-training modules for multi-role flexibility
Establish mentorship pairs between senior and junior technicians
Conduct simulation-based crisis response drills
review: Cross-training may dilute expertise if not balanced with specialized development.

name: Control Group Synchronization
consequences: Aligning control group protocols with experimental groups could improve comparative analysis but might require additional resources. A downstream effect is potential participant attrition from extended monitoring requirements.
options: Implement identical sleep environment conditions for control participants
Schedule control group assessments during peak event hours
Use identical compensation structures for both groups
review: Identical compensation structures may inadvertently bias control group demographics.

name: Regulatory Reporting Mechanism
consequences: Streamlining reporting processes could accelerate approvals but might reduce oversight depth. A downstream implication is potential compliance gaps during rapid expansions.
options: Automate routine compliance documentation with workflow software
Designate a dedicated regulatory liaison role
Create standardized audit checklists for external reviews
review: Automated documentation may create false assurance if not periodically manually validated.
